articles.title: Lula chama Haddad de 'joia' e diz que quem 'perde' com derrota de petista é o povo de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: O petista discursou em um hotel na regiao da Avenida Paulista após o resultado das eleições. Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) se enfrentarão no segundo turno no dia 25 de outubro.
articles.summary: O petista discursou em um hotel na regiao da Avenida Paulista após o resultado das eleições. Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) se enfrentarão no segundo turno no dia 25 de outubro.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula fala em SP após o resultado das eleições — Foto: João de Mari/g1

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) lamentou neste domingo (4) a derrota de Fernando Haddad (PT) à disputa do governo do estado de São Paulo. O petista discursou em um hotel na regiao da Avenida Paulista após o resultado das eleições. Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) se enfrentarão no segundo turno no dia 25 de outubro.

No discurso, Lula disse que o estado perdeu, pela terceira vez, a oportunidade de eleger Haddad. Pediu que o correligionário não desanime e afirmou que ele ainda terá a chance de mostrar sua capacidade de governar o estado ou o país.

"O Haddad é uma daquelas joias que o estado de São Paulo produziu. Haddad, não foi você que perdeu a eleição, foi o povo de São Paulo", disse.

E seguiu: "Me diga uma grande obra que está sendo pensada em São Paulo. As duas obras são pensadas com dinheiro do governo federal". "Não desanime, não. O teu dia chegará. E você vai poder mostrar que, se você conseguir governar este estado, este país, a gente vai dar um salto de qualidade."

O presidente também fez uma autocrítica sobre a estratégia política de seu grupo. Questionou se as decisões tomadas foram corretas e disse ser necessário repensar a forma como estão atuando.

Lula lamentou ainda as derrotas de Marina Silva e Simone Tebet na disputa pelo Senado em São Paulo . Destacou a atuação de Marina na agenda climática e a ligação de Tebet com o agronegócio e com pautas sociais.

Segundo Lula, as duas poderiam contribuir para temas como meio ambiente, inclusão social e distribuição de renda.

Lula encerrou reconhecendo que derrotas fazem parte da democracia e voltou à autocrítica: “Será que nós estamos errados? A história vai provar.”

Após a derrota para Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) na disputa pelo governo de São Paulo, Fernando Haddad (PT) afirmou neste domingo (4) que fez um “embate de alto nível” durante a campanha e desejou “o melhor” para o estado. O petista disse ainda que pretende atuar como oposição “da maneira mais construtiva possível” para melhorar as condições de vida da população.

Após a confirmação da vitória de Tarcísio, Haddad contou que ligou para o governador reeleito, às 19h11, para cumprimentá-lo e desejar boa sorte. Esta foi a segunda vez que Haddad disputou o governo de São Paulo. Em 2022, ele chegou ao segundo turno contra Tarcísio, mas terminou derrotado.

Fernando Haddad discursa para apoiadores após derrota, pela segunda vez, ao cargo de governador de São Paulo. — Foto: João de Mari/g1

“Eu liguei para o governador Tarcísio, cumprimentando, desejando boa sorte, reiterando que as críticas que eu fiz foram críticas programáticas, de um povo que pensa diferente, mas que quer o bem do estado”, afirmou.

Segundo Haddad, as críticas feitas durante a campanha foram baseadas em estudos e propostas e tinham como objetivo defender o que ele considera melhor para São Paulo.

"Críticas que foram estudadas com consistência, com coerência, com aquilo que a gente pensa que é o melhor para a sociedade paulista, o melhor para a sociedade brasileira", disse.

Haddad acompanhou a apuração no Hotel Meliá Paulista, na Avenida Paulista, na capital. Durante a apuração, o clima entre os apoiadores no hotel era de tensão. Os presentes acompanhavam a contagem dos votos pelo telão montado no local e demonstravam preocupação à medida que a vantagem de Tarcísio aumentava.

O petista afirmou ainda que pretende atuar como oposição de forma construtiva durante o próximo mandato de Tarcísio.

"Desejar o melhor para o nosso estado, nos colocar, enquanto oposição, da maneira mais construtiva possível para melhorar as condições de vida da nossa gente".

"Penso que nós fizemos um embate de alto nível, um embate digno do povo paulista".

Às 20h35, com 95,45% das urnas apuradas, Tarcísio tinha 62,71% dos votos válidos, contra 36,37% de Haddad.

O presidente estadual do PT em São Paulo, Kiko Celeguim, falou antes de Haddad e disse que o foco agora do diretório do partido no estado será acompanhar a campanha do presidente e candidato à reeleição Lula (PT) para o segundo turno. A candidata ao Senado Marina Silva (Rede), que não foi eleita, também participou da cerimônia após a confirmação do resultado.

Haddad chegou à campanha de 2026 como ex-ministro da Fazenda do governo Lula e voltou a disputar o governo paulista dois anos depois de ter sido derrotado por Tarcísio no segundo turno de 2022. O PT oficializou a candidatura em julho, em uma convenção em Campinas, com Márcio França (PSB) como candidato a vice-governador.

A campanha começou oficialmente em agosto, com Haddad ao lado de Lula em São Bernardo do Campo, cidade que é um dos principais símbolos da história do PT. Haddad voltou ao reduto petista na sexta-feira (2).

Desde os primeiros atos, o candidato buscou associar sua candidatura ao governo federal e apresentar a eleição estadual como uma disputa entre projetos diferentes para São Paulo.

As privatizações realizadas ou defendidas pelo governo Tarcísio estiveram entre os principais alvos de Haddad durante a campanha. O petista criticou a privatização da Sabesp e a concessão de serviços de transporte, além de explorar problemas registrados em serviços administrados por empresas privadas.

Nos debates entre os dois, na Band, em agosto, e na TV Globo, em setembro, privatizações, economia, segurança pública e a relação com o governo federal estiveram entre os principais temas do confronto.

Haddad também concentrou parte da campanha em propostas econômicas. Entre elas, defendeu a reindustrialização de São Paulo, a criação de um banco de desenvolvimento estadual inspirado no BNDES e maior aproximação entre universidades, Fapesp e empresas. Na reta final, afirmou que a formação profissional e o Ensino Médio deveriam ser adaptados às novas demandas da indústria.

Saúde, educação e segurança foram outros eixos da candidatura. Nas entrevistas e debates, Haddad criticou políticas do governo Tarcísio e apresentou propostas como a criação de uma agência de combate às facções criminosas, além de defender mudanças na organização da rede de saúde e investimentos em educação.

A campanha também foi marcada pela diferença no tempo de propaganda eleitoral. Tarcísio teve 6 minutos e 20 segundos de propaganda na televisão, enquanto Haddad contou com 2 minutos e 40 segundos, segundo dados do TRE-SP citados pelo candidato.

Dois dias antes da eleição, em uma agenda no Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos do ABC, Haddad afirmou que sua campanha havia “cumprido o seu objetivo” apesar do pouco tempo de TV e das poucas oportunidades de confronto . Segundo ele, a candidatura havia levado ao eleitor suas críticas à situação do estado nas áreas de segurança, saúde e educação.

Haddad em coletiva após debate — Foto: Globo/Bob Paulino

Fernando Haddad, de 63 anos, é advogado, professor e político do PT. Nascido em São Paulo, é filho de imigrantes libaneses e se formou em Direito pela Universidade de São Paulo (USP), onde também fez mestrado em Economia e doutorado em Filosofia. É professor do Departamento de Ciência Política da USP.

Sua trajetória no poder público começou na Prefeitura de São Paulo, onde foi subsecretário de Finanças durante a gestão de Marta Suplicy. No governo federal, trabalhou no Ministério do Planejamento e, em 2004, tornou-se secretário-executivo do Ministério da Educação. No ano seguinte, assumiu o comando da pasta, cargo que ocupou de 2005 a 2012, durante os governos Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva e Dilma Rousseff.

À frente do Ministério da Educação, Haddad participou da implementação e expansão de programas como o ProUni, o Sisu, o Enem e os institutos federais. Em 2012, deixou o governo federal para disputar a Prefeitura de São Paulo. Foi eleito no segundo turno e comandou a capital entre 2013 e 2016.

Na prefeitura, sua gestão teve como algumas de suas principais marcas políticas de mobilidade urbana, como a expansão das ciclovias e a revisão do Plano Diretor. Em 2016, tentou a reeleição, mas foi derrotado por João Doria (PSDB) no primeiro turno.

Dois anos depois, Haddad foi escolhido pelo PT para substituir Lula na disputa pela Presidência da República, depois que o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral barrou a candidatura do ex-presidente. Haddad chegou ao segundo turno, mas perdeu a eleição para Jair Bolsonaro.

Em 2022, voltou a disputar o governo de São Paulo. Chegou ao segundo turno contra Tarcísio de Freitas, mas terminou derrotado. Em 2023, assumiu o Ministério da Fazenda no terceiro governo Lula, onde permaneceu até março de 2026, quando deixou o cargo para disputar novamente o governo paulista.

Dos 19 governadores já eleitos no primeiro turno neste domingo (4), apenas uma mulher conseguiu chegar ao cargo. A única governadora eleita até aqui é Raquel Lyra (PSD) em Pernambuco . A candidata venceu a disputa no primeiro turno e garantiu um novo mandato à frente do estado.

Outras três mulheres avançaram para o 2º turno e seguem na disputa pelo comando de estados e do Distrito Federal.

No Acre, a ex-prefeita Maiza Assis (Progressistas) disputará o segundo turno contra Alan Rick (Republicanos).

No Distrito Federal, a vice-governadora Celina Leão (Progressistas) tentará se eleger governadora enfrentando Leandro Grass (PT).

Já em Tocantins, a senadora licenciada Professora Dorinha (União Brasil) segue na corrida pelo Palácio Araguaia e disputará votos com Vicentinho Júnior (PSDB).

O segundo turno das eleições será realizado no próximo 25 de outubro.

articles.title: Peça-chave na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, Fernanda tenta suavizar imagem do marido | G1
articles.standfirst: Cirurgiã-dentista mantinha perfil mais discreto antes das eleições e agora pode ser a próxima primeira-dama do Brasil.
articles.summary: Cirurgiã-dentista mantinha perfil mais discreto antes das eleições e agora pode ser a próxima primeira-dama do Brasil.
articles.body:
O candidato Flávio Bolsonaro e sua esposa Fernanda no palco da convenção do PL que oficializou a candidatura do senador à Presidência — Foto: Jean Carniel/Reuters

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) vai para o segundo turno para tentar ocupar a Presidência no lugar de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). Caso vença, o Brasil terá também uma nova primeira-dama: Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro.

Ocupando um papel central na campanha de Flávio durante o pleito, Fernanda teve a tarefa de suavizar a imagem do marido para o eleitorado feminino.

Sua participação foi ainda mais intensa porque o filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro não pôde contar com a participação ativa na campanha de sua madrasta, Michelle Bolsonaro .

Michelle e Flávio Bolsonaro em encontro em Brasília em 11 de agosto de 2026 — Foto: Vittor Sales/Divulgação

Depois de uma briga pública em junho deste ano, na qual Michelle acusou Flávio de maltratá-la por desavenças políticas, Fernanda assumiu um papel mais central, estrelando vídeos da campanha junto com Flávio, além de aumentar sua presença nas redes sociais.

A primeira publicação no perfil público de Fernanda no Instagram foi uma mensagem de Natal em dezembro de 2025, dirigida aos seguidores e apoiadores do marido, logo depois da oficialização da pré-candidatura de Flávio à Presidência.

Antes disso, a cirurgiã-dentista de 45 anos mantinha um perfil mais discreto. Filha de médicos, Fernanda é casada com Flávio desde 2010. O casal tem duas filhas, Luiza e Carolina. Ambos se conheceram e moraram até 2019 no Rio de Janeiro, mudando-se depois para Brasília, quando Flávio assumiu mandato de senador.

Dois anos depois, o casal comprou uma mansão de R$ 5,97 milhões em Brasília . Metade do valor foi pago à vista e o restante foi financiado junto ao Banco de Brasília (BRB). Em três anos, o casal quitou o financiamento.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a esposa, Fernanda, e o pastor Silas Malafaia em ato na Avenida Paulista — Foto: THIAGO MIYASHIRO/PERA PHOTO PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Com a mudança, Fernanda montou um consultório em uma clínica no Lago Sul, na capital federal, onde continua atendendo pacientes. Segundo a equipe de campanha do marido, sua carreira incluiu ainda uma passagem pela Aeronáutica. Em 2009, Fernanda ingressou na Força como cirurgiã-dentista e atuou como tenente durante oito anos, segundo sua assessoria de imprensa.

Fernanda acompanhou o marido à posse do presidente chileno, José Antonio Kast — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

A ida de Fernanda ao lado do marido foi divulgada pela MiThi, agência do publicitário Thiago Miranda – elo entre o presidenciável e Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, que está preso e financiou o filme Dark Horse, que conta a história de Jair Bolsonaro.

À época, a agência de Miranda encaminhou a veículos de comunicação uma sugestão de pauta com o título: “Fernanda Bolsonaro leva renda nordestina ao Chile em evento diplomático”.

Ao g1 , Miranda negou que esteja trabalhando na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro para a presidência da República, mas afirmou ser próximo ao casal.

“Não tenho nenhum tipo de contrato com ele [Flávio], nem com a Fernanda. São pessoas do meu ciclo, pessoas que eu gosto, pessoas que eu tenho um relacionamento, mas trabalho formal, trabalhar na campanha, no dia a dia, não”, declarou o publicitário.

Com a ausência de Michelle na pré-campanha e ainda antes da briga pública, Flávio e o PL já começaram a apostar em Fernanda na narrativa eleitoral.

O candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) discursa no palco da convenção do partido neste sábado (25) — Foto: Jean Carniel/Reuters

Em um vídeo publicado em abril, Flávio conta como sua história com a mulher começou, antes da entrada dos dois na vida pública. O candidato à Presidência contou que eles se conheceram durante uma excursão de ônibus para Arraial d'Ajuda, na Bahia.

Segundo Flávio, foi “paixão à primeira vista”. Fernanda teria dito “eu te amo” apenas três dias depois de se conhecerem.

Em meio ao conflito público entre Flávio e Michelle, ela saiu em defesa do marido e escreveu que, como esposa, escolhia olhar para o homem que via diariamente: “um homem leve, respeitoso, carinhoso, restaurado”.

A participação de Fernanda ganhou ainda mais espaço na convenção nacional do PL, que confirmou a candidatura do senador à Presidência. Ela foi chamada pelo marido para discursar, momento no qual se apresentou como mulher, mãe, cirurgiã-dentista e brasileira, e afirmou que queria “mudança para esse Brasil”.

Fernanda Bolsonaro discursou antes do marido na convenção partidária do PL — Foto: Reprodução/Youtube

Em outro vídeo de campanha, veiculado em agosto, Fernanda afirmou ter ajudado a “reeducar” o marido e o descreveu como um “Bolsonaro moderado”. O discurso está alinhado com a estratégia do candidato para se aproximar das eleitoras mulheres e dos indecisos.

Flávio chegou a ser apontado pelo Ministério Público do Rio de Janeiro como chefe de uma organização criminosa que atuou em seu gabinete no período em que foi deputado na Alerj. Entre 2003 e 2018, ele cumpriu quatro mandatos parlamentares consecutivos.

A estimativa é que cerca de R$ 2,3 milhões tenham sido desviados no esquema. A Justiça do Rio, no entanto, recusou apresentar denúncia contra Flávio.

🔎 Rachadinha foi o nome dado para o esquema no qual parte ou a totalidade do salário de funcionários públicos são "devolvidos" para o parlamentar ou desviados para outras pessoas. A prática ilegal pode envolver ainda funcionários fantasmas, ou seja, que não trabalham realmente no gabinete.

Fernanda também é citada em uma investigação da Polícia Federal envolvendo o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro. Em 2025, a PF encontrou no celular do ex-presidente um arquivo de 33 páginas com um rascunho de pedido de asilo político ao presidente da Argentina, Javier Milei.

A ligação com Fernanda surgiu a partir dos metadados do arquivo. O documento tinha como criador e último autor o usuário “FERNANDA BOLSONARO”. No relatório, a Polícia Federal afirmou que “é possível” que esse usuário estivesse vinculado a Fernanda Bolsonaro.

“Nesse sentido, é possível que o usuário em questão esteja vinculado à pessoa de Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, nora do ex-presidente e esposa do senador Flavio Nantes Bolsonaro”, diz o relatório da PF.

O texto encontrado no celular pedia a concessão de asilo político a Bolsonaro na Argentina e alegava que ele era vítima de perseguição política no Brasil. Para a PF, o documento fazia parte de elementos que indicavam risco de fuga do ex-presidente.

A defesa de Bolsonaro, porém, afirmou que ele recebeu a sugestão de pedir asilo à Argentina, mas não aderiu à ideia.

Depois da condenação e prisão de Bolsonaro por tentativa de golpe de Estado pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Fernanda tentou ser designada a dentista do sogro.

Em agosto de 2026, a defesa de Bolsonaro pediu ao STF autorização para que ele deixasse a prisão domiciliar para uma consulta odontológica . A profissional indicada pelos advogados para realizar o atendimento era Fernanda, mulher de Flávio.

O pedido foi feito em meio à proibição de visitas de Flávio ao pai. Em julho, o ministro Alexandre de Moraes havia determinado que o senador ficasse 90 dias sem visitar Bolsonaro, após considerar que houve descumprimento das condições da prisão domiciliar com a divulgação de uma carta do ex-presidente em apoio à candidatura do filho.

O ex-presidente foi atendido em agosto, no Centro Odontológico da Polícia Militar do Distrito Federal. A defesa havia pedido que o procedimento fosse realizado no consultório de Fernanda, no Lago Sul, mas o pedido foi negado.

articles.title: Jeffries: House Democrats ‘poised to take back the majority’
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday that Democrats are on the path to reclaiming the majority in the lower chamber of Congress. Jeffries, during a conference call, told reporters the upcoming midterms are similar to those in 2018, when Democrats took back the House during President Trump’s first term, The Associated Press reported.…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday that Democrats are on the path to reclaiming the majority in the lower chamber of Congress.

Jeffries, during a conference call, told reporters the upcoming midterms are similar to those in 2018, when Democrats took back the House during President Trump’s first term, The Associated Press reported.

“House Democrats are poised to take back the majority,” the New York Democrat continued, according to the AP.

Democrats have a pretty rosy electoral outlook for November, with Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasting that they’ll hit 234 seats in the lower chamber after the upcoming midterms and retake the House. Republicans, on the other hand, are dealing with issues like President Trump’s sagging approval rating , the unpopular war in Iran and affordability concerns with Election Day just a month away.

According to DDHQ’s polling average, Trump’s approval rating sits at 38.6 percent, as of Monday morning, with his disapproval rating at 59.3 percent.

A recent Quinnipiac University survey also found that 51 percent of registered voters say if the midterms were held now, they would want Democrats to lock down the House majority, while 39 percent said the same about Republicans.

Trump on Saturday pressed his supporters to go to the polls for the midterms, vowing a “big” GOP victory if they did so.

“You got to get out and vote. You got to get out. You got to vote for these guys,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at a rally in Ohio.

“Just get out and vote. If you do that, we’re gonna win and we’re gonna win big and we’re gonna shove it up their a‑‑,” the president added.

The remarks came as part of his red state campaign blitz . Trump and Vice President Vance have been active in the field stumping for vulnerable GOP candidates and incumbents in recent weeks.

articles.title: Disgraced ex-GOP Speaker Dennis Hastert dies at 84
articles.summary: John Dennis Hastert (R-Ill.), the former House Speaker who later went to prison for charges related to allegations of sexual abuse against underaged boys, died over the weekend at his home “due to natural causes,” according to Illinois’ Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell. Hastert, who died at 84, served as the speaker of the House…
articles.body:
John Dennis Hastert (R-Ill.), the former House Speaker who later went to prison for charges related to allegations of sexual abuse against underaged boys, died over the weekend at his home “due to natural causes,” according to Illinois’ Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.

Hastert, who died at 84, served as the speaker of the House from 1999 to 2007, until Democrats won back the House and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) succeeded him. He announced that he would not seek reelection in 2008, ending his tenure in Congress.

During his Speakership, Hastert helped to enact some of the most consequential legislation of the last half-century, including two rounds of massive tax cuts that were the signature domestic achievement of President George W. Bush. Hastert was also in power during the 9/11 attacks and oversaw the launch of the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Bush had said then that he was “indebted to Denny for his candid advice and strong support.”

But his legacy was quickly overshadowed by the revelations that he had paid hush money to a man alleging that Hastert had sexually abused him when Hastert was a high school wrestling coach in Illinois decades earlier. The payments led federal prosecutors to open a broader investigation into allegations that Hastert had abused at least four boys at the school.

The judge in the case characterized Hastert as a “serial child molester,” but the statute of limitations surrounding the abuse allegations had long expired by the time of the investigation.

In 2015, he pleaded guilty to financial crimes related to the scandal, thereby avoiding a long and potentially embarrassing trial. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison in 2016, and spent 13 months behind bars.

Amid the revelations, former Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) removed Hastert’s portrait from the Speaker’s lobby of the U.S. Capitol, a hallowed hallway just off the House floor where the pictures of dozens of past Speakers are displayed.

Hastert was born and raised in rural Illinois, where he was a standout athlete before becoming a high school teacher and coach while in his early twenties. In 1976, after leading the school’s wrestling team to a state championship, he was named the state’s coach of the year.

He left teaching five years later, after winning a seat in the Illinois House, where he served for three terms before being elected to the U.S. House in 1986.

His rise to the Speakership was a surprise, coming only after a series of stunning events shook Washington in the late 1990s.

The first of those was the 1998 elections, a mid-term cycle when Republicans were expecting big gains amid the Monica Lewinsky scandal that dogged then-President Bill Clinton. Instead, Democrats gained seats, forcing the GOP’s powerhouse Speaker, Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), to step out of power.

Rep. Bob Livingston (R-La.), was elected to succeed Gingrich, but Livingston never took the gavel after revelations of an extramarital affair, clearing the way for Hastert.

From that perch, Hastert helped Bush push through major parts of his ambitious agenda, including the tax cuts of 2001 and 2003.

He also adopted an informal policy that no legislation would be considered by the chamber unless it had the support of more than half of all the Republicans. Known as the “Hastert rule,” the policy remains a powerful influence in the House to this day.

articles.title: Live updates: Supreme Court opens term with climate change case

Suncor v. Boulder is an appeal of a Colorado Supreme Court decision that allowed claims…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court opens its new term on Monday with oral arguments in a major climate case that could determine the future of state and local efforts to recover damages from fossil fuel companies over their role in global warming.

Suncor v. Boulder is an appeal of a Colorado Supreme Court decision that allowed claims of climate damages brought by the city and county against oil companies to proceed. The Trump administration has joined the energy companies, who argue that arguing that federal law preempts state level cases on the issue.

President Trump on Monday will head to Grand Island, Neb. , for the latest stop in his red state campaign swing as he pushes for Republicans to maintain both chambers of Congress. In the last week, he’s stumped in Texas, Oklahoma , Alabama and Ohio . He’ll return to Texas and Alabama this week, too.

Vice President Vance will try to boost the chances of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) at a rally in Anchorage, Alaska , a rare high-level campaign stop in the Frontier State. Sullivan is in a tight reelection contest with former Rep. Mary Peltola (R-Alaska).

articles.title: Cruz labels Vance ‘insecure’ after 2028 remarks
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), seen as a possible 2028 candidate, has criticized Vice President Vance over his recent remarks that the GOP senator was clearing positioning himself for a White House bid, calling the comments “political bomb-throwing” and the vice president “insecure.” “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz told Politico…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), seen as a possible 2028 candidate, has criticized Vice President Vance over his recent remarks that the GOP senator was clearing positioning himself for a White House bid, calling the comments “political bomb-throwing” and the vice president “insecure.”

“In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz told Politico in an interview on Saturday.

“So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes,” he continued. “I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.”

Last week, the vice president told NBC News it was “really obvious” that “Ted Cruz is running for president,” before adding that he was more focused on helping Republicans win the midterms.

Cruz told Politico over the weekend that he’s also helped campaign for a number of candidates this cycle in states like Georgia and Nebraska, while pointing out that he also campaigned for the vice president when he first ran for Ohio Senate in 2022.

“I was very glad he won that race,” Cruz said. “I was very glad to help him.”

The Hill has reached out to a Vance spokesperson for comment.

Vance is seen as the frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination in 2028 given his status as vice president. He and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have dominated the early discussion about who might succeed President Trump, a conversation the president himself has sparked with his own comments about the two men.

Cruz, however, has invited speculation that he, too, is thinking of running again for the White House after losing to President Trump in the 2016 GOP primary.

Cruz endorsed candidates in the midterms, including backing some challengers of Trump endorsees like Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and South Carolina gubernatorial candidate Alan Wilson, both of whom won their primaries.

“I’ll certainly be part of the discussion,” Cruz told MS NOW in August regarding the 2028 field. He also suggested Vance didn’t have a lock on the 2028 GOP presidential primary.

Other Republicans who have started to invite speculation over their next steps have included Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Blanche and Hegseth have both waved off the idea they’re interested in running in two years.

articles.title: Extreme heat in prisons is cruel, unusual and unconstitutional
articles.summary: A federal judge has ruled that not having air conditioning in Deep South prisons violates the Constitution Eighth Amendment.
articles.body:
Millions of Americans live without air conditioning . Estimates put that number as high as 35 million . And, as Professor Nambi Ndugga and his colleagues report, “Asian, Black, and Hispanic- led households are more likely to report not having an air conditioning unit in their home compared to white households and keeping their homes at unsafe or unhealthy temperatures.”

Such conditions are especially prevalent in American prisons, particularly in Deep South states like Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. In those prisons, summertime temperatures can routinely reach triple digits.

A report from the Prison Policy Institute notes that prisons “are mostly built from heat-retaining materials, which can increase internal prison temperatures. Because of this, the temperatures inside prisons can often exceed outdoor temperatures.”

“Moreover,” it continues, citing a report in Prison Legal News, “‘people outside of prison who experience extreme heat have options that prisoners often lack — they can take a cool shower, drink cold water, move into the shade, or go to a place that is air conditioned. For prisoners, those options are generally unavailable.’”

On Sept. 22, Robert Pitman, a federal district judge in Texas, ruled that the failure to provide cooling in the Lone Star State’s prisons constituted a form of cruel and unusual punishment that is prohibited by the Constitution. He was right to do so, and his opinion should be a model for judges in other states.

Some might think that Pitman must be an out-of-control judicial activist, more sympathetic to the plight of hardened criminals than ordinary Americans. But nothing could be further from the truth.

Pitman was following long-established judicial precedents that impose special obligations on the government when it takes someone into its custody. Even the conservative former Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist recognized that “in certain limited circumstances, the Constitution imposes upon the State affirmative duties of care and protection with respect to particular individuals.”

Prisoners, Rehnquist noted, were included among the people to whom such a duty of care is owed.

Although judges have long recognized that prisons don’t have to be comfortable places , they have also recognized that they cannot be unhealthy ones . Some judges have said that “prisoners retain all rights enjoyed by free citizens except those necessarily lost as an incident of confinement.”

Prisons impinge on the rights of inmates who are forced to live in the extreme heat of a Deep South summer, according to the Prison Policy Initiative . “The lack of air conditioning in Southern prisons creates unsafe — even lethal — conditions. Prolonged exposure to extreme heat can cause dehydration and heat stroke, both of which can be fatal. It can also affect people’s kidneys, liver, heart, brain, and lungs, which can lead to renal failure, heart attack, and stroke.”

As Pitman put it, “inmates in Texas prisons are suffering — and in some cases dying. … These,” he added — of the condition in prisons when the state reaches triple-digit heat index readings — “are not humane conditions.”

The judge faulted state officials for not responding “reasonably to address extreme heat in Texas’s un-air-conditioned prisons…” and for “fail[ing] to meaningfully investigate and document prison temperatures and their effects, underrepresenting the scope of the problem.”

Pitman found that “even where heat conditions do not result in immediate injuries or death, the heat in Texas prisons creates degrading, inhumane conditions and causes severe suffering.” That is familiar language in cases on the meaning of the constitutional prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment.

He also points out that Texas takes better care of its farm animals than its prisoners, spending “millions of dollars to ensure that poultry are housed in safe temperatures. … These protections do not exist in inmate housing facilities.”

Pitman’s decision, if it is upheld on appeal, will not be an easy or cheap one for Texas to implement. Estimates of the cost run in the neighborhood of $1.5 billion.

Decisions protecting the rights of prisoners are seldom popular with people who are asked to foot the bill, or who think that the suffering of prisoners is the price they pay for the suffering they impose on others. That is why it is as important as it has ever been for judges to do what Pitman did.

Air conditioning in Texas prisons is hardly a sign that anyone is soft on crime. It is, instead, a testament to our commitment to the dignity and worth of everyone — even those whose crimes justify their incarceration.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Tillis warns of ‘risk’ Trump will lash out if Republicans have bad night in midterms
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) says there’s a “risk” that President Trump will lash out if Republicans lose control of the House and possibly the Senate as well in next month’s election. Asked by Ross Douthat during an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” whether he had concerns about Trump’s reaction if Republicans have a “bad night”…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) says there’s a “risk” that President Trump will lash out if Republicans lose control of the House and possibly the Senate as well in next month’s election.

Asked by Ross Douthat during an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” whether he had concerns about Trump’s reaction if Republicans have a “bad night” on Nov. 3, Election Day, Tillis replied: “I think there’s a risk, I really do.”

And Tillis warned it would be a mistake for Trump to attack members of his own party or to dispute the results of the election if they lose badly when polls show that the president’s low approval rating and voters’ concern over affordability are two of the biggest factors influencing the polls.

“It would be another political unforced error if we do that,” he said.

Tillis’s comments came as part of a discussion about Trump’s efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, which led up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

The North Carolina senator said he’s still disgusted thinking back to that day of chaos on Capitol Hill, when a mob of pro-Trump supporters stormed the Senate and House chambers.

“Look, this was the first time in the history of this country that we had not had a completely peaceful transfer of power on that day. And that was despicable,” he said. “The people that led the charge, the people that assaulted police officers, I wish they were still in prison and serving a very long sentence.”

Yet, Tillis defended his vote to acquit Trump on the charge of inciting insurrection, arguing that Democrats rushed the impeachment proceedings and pushed the charge to prevent the president from running for office again in 2024.

“What you’re doing is a means-justifies-the-end rationalization. So cheapening the impeachment process to prevent someone from running in the future, I just don’t buy it,” he said.

Trump has warned for months of what he insists is a possibility of widespread fraud in this year’s election even though there are few substantiated instances of voter fraud in recent federal elections.

Trump pushed Republicans for much of this year to pass the SAVE America Act , which would require voters to present photo identification to vote and require people to provide documented proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

The president also issued an executive order in March tasking the U.S. Postal Service with screening out mail-in ballots that did not match voter lists compiled by the Department of Homeland Security. Courts have blocked this plan.

And Trump, in an interview with Time magazine published last week, declined to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections.

“I’m not committing to anything,” he said. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”

articles.title: Trump takes aim at the free press ahead of midterms
articles.summary: President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have faced criticism for actions perceived as undermining the freedom of the press and withholding information regarding the ongoing war in Iran.
articles.body:
Does President Trump really control a video channel? Yes. That’s not hype — it is true. The YouTube channel is being advertised as showing his “biggest moments all in one place.”

“Quite literally state-run TV,” said California Gov. Gavin Newsom , a Democrat.

Also, hard to believe but true, is that in the last few days President Trump used taxpayer money to run political ads on television framing him as the nation’s hero.

There is more. For the first time in history the president controls a social media platform, Truth Social. He recently tried to charge a fee for early access to his presidential announcements on the site. And Trump is blaming the press for polls showing his party doing badly in the midterm elections. He is lashing out, getting even, with an assault on the First Amendment protection for a free press.

Trump wants to energize his voters by demonizing the press. He recently pulled White House passes from reporters for three media companies. He announced the punishment on Truth Social and identified the targeted outlets as “Fake News” organizations.

Trump’s effort to control the news extends to coverage of the war in Iran.

That fighting is now more than six months along. But the Pentagon has not held a press briefing since May .

And last month, the Washington Post reported that the Pentagon hid full reporting on the extent of casualties in the war.

Four people killed in combat had not been counted as casualties as the Trump administration attempted to “portray the war as a success,” the Post reported . The Pentagon had “reclassified,” some deaths. Those deaths of those soldiers did not count, according to the Pentagon, because they took place in a separate phase of combat.

More unsettling revelations about the administration’s carefully shaped image of the war emerged last week.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told military leaders last week that news reports about declining levels of arms stockpiles and poor morale among troops are “anti-American.” He called these reports acts of “partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they’re undertaking … it’s sick. It’s a national betrayal. It’s treason, actually.”

Keep in mind that members of the U.S. military swear an oath to the Constitution, not to a president or a political party. That constitution includes the First Amendment.

Last year, Hegseth imposed strict restrictions on reporters moving around the Pentagon. That prompted virtually all major news organizations to surrender their Pentagon press passes and leave.

Hegseth later replaced them with his hand-selected group of reporters.

“The Pentagon has secretly installed several conservative military veterans with large online followings in government roles,” the Washington Post reported in August. The influencers’ job is to “amplify … Hegseth’s viewpoints and attack those who scrutinize the Trump administration,” the paper reported.

News stories from several outlets reported this summer about crisis conditions among sailors on an American aircraft carrier that had been at sea for nine months. Hegseth dismissed those stories as “completely misrepresented.”

The president supported Hegseth’s appraisal by saying the ship’s deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

Last week, the Navy conceded that eight sailors had attempted suicide on that ship.

The consequences of attacks on independent American journalism is not abstract. A free press at the Pentagon is vital to voters’ understanding of the war as they vote in the midterms. Government-controlled press reports amount to propaganda. They undercut the basic premise of an informed electorate freely choosing its leaders.

Trump’s offensive against the free press extends to bragging that he can get better ratings than independent news organizations. His midterm Republican convention got “107 million views,” he claimed . He said that number surpassed the number of viewers for an NFL game that was aired at the same time.

Let the record show that he got 2.5 million viewers while the NFL got more than 25 million.

When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the White House last month, Trump praised the Chinese reporters as the “friendliest press corps.” He did not mention that the Chinese have no First Amendment protection for a free press. He made no reference to the heavy-handed censorship of the press in China. Trump merely made Chinese state-controlled press into a positive model for the American press.

That fit with comments he made earlier this year when confronted with the historical pattern of midterm losses for the party in power. Trump told Reuters : “When you think of it, we shouldn’t even have an election.” It is hard to believe, but he said it.

Maybe that is why conspiracy theories about potential election tricks by Trump continue to circulate.

The basic script is clear: Republicans could seek to delay or prevent the seating of members from closely contested districts, citing bogus allegations of voter fraud or unresolved election disputes.

Trump is likely to blame “fake news,” for reports about any political maneuvering to weaken any defeat in the elections.

As Thomas Jefferson famously wrote from Paris in his 1787 letter to Edward Carrington, given the choice, he would prefer “newspapers without a government” over “a government without newspapers.”

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Karoline Leavitt joining Fox News
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt, President Trump’s former White House press secretary is set to join Fox News next month as a contributor. Leavitt, the only person to serve as the president’s top spokesperson during his second term, will join a number of other former Trump administration officials and allies at the network, according to The New York…
articles.body:
Karoline Leavitt, President Trump’s former White House press secretary is set to join Fox News next month as a contributor.

Leavitt, the only person to serve as the president’s top spokesperson during his second term, will join a number of other former Trump administration officials and allies at the network, according to The New York Times .

She gave birth to her second child this summer and weeks later announced she would leave the administration to spend more time with her family.

Leavitt was known during her time at the podium for her fierce defense of Trump’s policies and frequent sparring with reporters in the White House briefing room.

She joins another former White House press secretary, Kaleigh McEnany, at the outlet, where she is expected to provide commentary and analysis across a number of the channel’s news and opinion programs, the Times reported.

As he built his second Cabinet, Trump tapped a long list of former Fox News personalities and hosts to fill key positions in his administration, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and others.

A former Republican House candidate in New Hampshire, Leavitt served as the top spokesperson for the president’s reelection campaign and was the youngest person to ever serve as White House press secretary when she was selected for the job.

Leavitt is set to begin at Fox on Nov. 1.

articles.title: Supreme Court won’t reinstate Pennsylvania judge suspended for partisan Facebook posts
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a former Pennsylvania judge’s challenge to his suspension for making partisan Facebook posts, a dispute that touches on issues of free speech and judicial ethics. Pennsylvania’s judicial discipline board suspended then-Judge Mark Cohen in 2024 over dozens of posts praising Democrats, including former President Biden and Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), and his advocacy…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a former Pennsylvania judge’s challenge to his suspension for making partisan Facebook posts, a dispute that touches on issues of free speech and judicial ethics.

Pennsylvania’s judicial discipline board suspended then-Judge Mark Cohen in 2024 over dozens of posts praising Democrats, including former President Biden and Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), and his advocacy for policies such as raising the minimum wage.

Cohen previously served more than four decades in the Pennsylvania legislature and ran for the judgeship as a Democrat. He casts the Facebook posts as him continuing to express his views on matters of public concern. He argues lower courts used too lenient a First Amendment standard to uphold his suspension.

“This Court’s guidance is sorely needed,” his attorneys wrote in his petition. “If allowed to stand, the Cohen decision will have a chilling effect on judicial speech, invite political interference in the judicial branch, undermine the rule of law, and have the perverse effect of impugning the integrity of the judiciary.”

Cohen also lost his pensions, court filings show.

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court applied a balancing test typically used when a government worker argues their employer disciplined them in violation of their free speech rights.

Cohen argues judges are public officials speaking to their constituents, not an ordinary employee.

“This Court should grant the petition because it cleanly presents a question of importance concerning fundamental First Amendment protections for members of the judiciary,” his lawyers at DLA Piper wrote.

Pennsylvania’s Judicial Conduct Board, represented by Stanford Law School’s Supreme Court Litigation Clinic, called Cohen’s posts “partisan cheerleading” and said there is no precedent supporting that judges can do so under their First Amendment rights.

“There is no reason for this Court to review that straightforward application of familiar rules that judges around the country have followed for decades,” they wrote in court filings.

articles.title: Supreme Court declines to take up school ban on ‘Let’s Go Brandon’ shirts
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will not hear a dispute over whether a Michigan public school district can bar students from wearing clothing emblazoned with “Let’s Go Brandon,” a popular conservative slogan used to mock former President Biden. The justices declined on Monday to take up a request from two brothers who claim their First Amendment rights…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court will not hear a dispute over whether a Michigan public school district can bar students from wearing clothing emblazoned with “Let’s Go Brandon,” a popular conservative slogan used to mock former President Biden.

The justices declined on Monday to take up a request from two brothers who claim their First Amendment rights were violated when they were told to remove sweatshirts with the slogan because it violated the school’s policy against profanity.

The brothers, identified as D.A. and X.A, were in sixth and eighth grade, respectively, at the time. They are now enrolled in a high school in the same school district, Tri County Schools, which is located roughly 30 miles north of Grand Rapids.

Lawyers for the pair’s mother, who sued the school district and two middle school employees in 2023 on behalf of her sons, argued the apparel is protected political speech and cannot be censored so long as it is not disruptive.

A federal judge sided with the school district, finding that the school could prohibit students from wearing the slogan because it amounted to vulgar speech. A split panel for the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed .

“In the schoolhouse, vulgarity trumps politics,” the appeals court majority wrote. “And the protection for political speech doesn’t give a student carte blanche to use vulgarity at school —even when that vulgarity is cloaked in innuendo or euphemism.”

In their petition to the high court, lawyers contended that the appeals court misunderstood Fraser, a 1986 case that found the First Amendment does not prevent school districts from prohibiting vulgar and lewd speech.

They pointed to a dissent from 6th Circuit Judge John Bush, who wrote that his colleagues’ decision “essentially gives school administrators boundless discretion” to censor political speech.

“The Sixth Circuit’s decision deepens confusion and disagreement in the lower courts on an issue affecting tens of millions of public school students: What political apparel does the First Amendment protect at school?” the students’ lawyers wrote.

The school district, however, argued the slogan’s apparent meaning as a euphemism for “F— Joe Biden” cannot be ignored.

“Fraser holds that school administrators can restrict speech touching on political topics when that speech is vulgar, profane, or lewd — even when expressed in euphemisms,” its lawyers wrote. “A contrary rule would allow vulgar, lewd, and profane codewords to flood classrooms and would prevent schools from teaching students how to engage in political discussions with civility.”

The phrase originated from a 2021 NASCAR event in which a reporter who was interviewing a racecar driver incorrectly interpreted the crowd’s derogatory chant about Biden to be “Let’s Go Brandon.” The clip went viral, and the slogan was quickly embraced by conservatives as a way to express opposition to the Biden administration.

The Supreme Court has declined to take up similar cases before, including last year when it said it would not review whether a Massachusetts school district had violated a student’s constitutional rights by blocking him from wearing a “There are only two genders” shirt.

articles.title: Supreme Court declines to hear convicted sex cult leader Keith Rainere’s appeal
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to take up an appeal from Keith Raniere challenging his conviction on racketeering and sex-trafficking charges in connection with his leadership of the NXIVM sex cult. The decision leaves in place an October ruling from a federal appeals court panel that upheld the verdict and a decades-long prison sentence…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to take up an appeal from Keith Raniere challenging his conviction on racketeering and sex-trafficking charges in connection with his leadership of the NXIVM sex cult.

The decision leaves in place an October ruling from a federal appeals court panel that upheld the verdict and a decades-long prison sentence that was handed down in 2020.

A federal jury in New York found Raniere guilty on seven counts in June 2019, following a six-week trial that centered on allegations that he operated the secretive group as a criminal enterprise that engaged in forced labor, as well as the exploitation and abuse of young girls.

Raniere founded NXIVM in Albany, N.Y., in the early 2000s as a purported self-help organization that offered expensive workshops based on his teachings in centers across the U.S., Canada and Mexico.

He created a secret society within the organization called DOS, or “The Vow,” that separated women into “slaves” and “masters,” intended to promote Raniere’s ideology and recruit new members, according to prosecutors.

They said Raniere, who went by “Vanguard,” controlled his followers by collecting “collateral,” such as explicit photos or embarrassing information, that he then used to manipulate them into forced labor or sexual acts with him.

In some cases, DOS “slaves” were branded on their pelvises with Raniere’s initials. The group also held a woman captive in a room for nearly two years, according to prosecutors, among other crimes.

Raniere was sentenced to 120 years in prison and ordered to pay a $1.75 million fine. More than a dozen victims offered personal testimony at his sentencing hearing, including a woman named “Camila” who was sexually abused by Raniere at the age of 15.

He has sought a new trial on the grounds that FBI agents fabricated evidence of child pornography that was used against him at trial. He alleges that nude photographs of “Camila” were planted on a hard drive and camera memory card that were seized from his townhouse and certain information was withheld from the defense.

Raniere’s repeated attempts to overturn the conviction have been rejected at both the trial and appellate court levels. The U.S. Supreme Court also turned away an earlier appeal in 2023.

articles.title: Supreme Court ends Charleston church shooter’s bid to disqualify trial judge
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear the Charleston church massacre shooter’s attempt to disqualify his trial judge from further proceedings over claims that he failed to remain impartial. The high court’s decision leaves intact an appeals court ruling that found no basis to remove U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel from the death-penalty…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear the Charleston church massacre shooter’s attempt to disqualify his trial judge from further proceedings over claims that he failed to remain impartial.

The high court’s decision leaves intact an appeals court ruling that found no basis to remove U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel from the death-penalty case against convicted shooter Dylann Roof.

Roof, now 32, was convicted of federal hate crime and related charges for opening fire on a group of parishioners who were gathered for Bible study at the historic Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, S.C., in May 2015. Nine people were killed. Five people survived the attack.

The self-proclaimed white supremacist was sentenced to death in 2017 for the massacre, which he confessed was intended to spark a race war.

Roof, who represented himself in the sentencing phase, has mounted multiple unsuccessful attempts to overturn his conviction and get a new trial in the decade since. The Supreme Court had already denied taking up his appeal once , in 2022.

The new challenge focused on the ongoing post-conviction proceedings, which Roof’s lawyers argued Gergel should be removed from due to a “constitutionally unacceptable appearance of bias” in the matter. The allegation stems from a conversation in which lawyers say Gergel expressed a desire to handle the trial.

“In granting the petition, this Court will not disturb the underlying convictions or sentence, but rather ensure confidence in our judiciary and the resolution of the claims in this case with no appearance of partiality,” Roof’s lawyers wrote in its petition. “A case like this one, which remains under scrutiny of the victims and the public, demands no less.”

The judicial bias issue was raised with the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which held last year that Roof had not shown a “clear and indisputable right to recusal” after finding his allegations that Gergel wanted the case from the beginning were insufficient and based on hearsay.

The Trump administration had urged the Supreme Court not to get involved again, writing that the appeals court’s order did not warrant further review.

Roof is housed in a high-security prison in Terre Haute, Ind. He was one of three federal death-row inmates whose sentence was not commuted to life in prison by former President Joe Biden on his way out of office.

articles.title: Supreme Court won’t hear Roy Moore’s appeal over $8.2 million jury verdict in campaign ad dispute
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a challenge from Roy Moore, the former Alabama Supreme Court justice, to an appeals court ruling that wiped out a multi-million defamation verdict over a 2017 campaign ad that recounted allegations of sexual misconduct against him. The decision effectively ends Moore’s long-running legal battle against Senate Majority…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a challenge from Roy Moore, the former Alabama Supreme Court justice, to an appeals court ruling that wiped out a multi-million defamation verdict over a 2017 campaign ad that recounted allegations of sexual misconduct against him.

The decision effectively ends Moore’s long-running legal battle against Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic-aligned political action committee. The justices also turned away his emergency appeal to review the lower court order earlier this year without explanation.

The dispute centered on television commercials aired by Highway 31, a group backed by the Senate Majority PAC, during a 2017 special election that suggested Moore was banned from a local mall for soliciting sex from teenage girls.

The ads cited news reports detailing accusations of sexual misconduct by several women, including one woman who claimed Moore initiated a sexual encounter with her when she was 14, and he was in his 30s. Moore has denied the allegations.

The former judge, who was running as the GOP nominee for former Sen. Jeff Sessions’ seat in the Senate, ultimately lost the race to Democrat Doug Jones.

Moore sued the PAC and several others for defamation and invasion of privacy, arguing the commercials were misleading and falsely implied that he had solicited sex from a 14-year-old.

He was initially awarded $8.2 million by an Alabama jury in 2022, but a three-judge panel for the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the verdict after finding that Moore had failed to meet the “actual malice” standard created by New York Times v. Sullivan.

That standard requires public figures suing for defamation prove that the publisher knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.

Moore’s lawyers had asked the Supreme Court to take another look.

“The repercussions extend far beyond this case,” they wrote in their petition.

“Modern political ads are built from excerpts of statements. If a publisher can escape a jury’s verdict by accurately quoting each fragment while manufacturing a false whole, Masson’s core holding is nullified for the very media where fabrication is easiest and most damaging,” his lawyers continued, referencing the 1991 Supreme Court precedent that established deliberately altering a direct quote does not amount to defamation unless it changes the factual meaning.

The Senate Majority PAC did not file a response to Moore’s petition.

articles.title: De Niro calls Trump a ‘coward,’ ‘piece of s—‘
articles.summary: Robert De Niro is slamming President Trump, calling the commander in chief a “coward” and “piece of s—” in expletive-laden remarks and urging voters to “take back the power” in next month’s elections. “Power to the people isn’t just a slogan — it’s the founding principle of our nation, guaranteed by the Constitution,” the “Irishman”…
articles.body:
Robert De Niro is slamming President Trump, calling the commander in chief a “coward” and “piece of s—” in expletive-laden remarks and urging voters to “take back the power” in next month’s elections.

“Power to the people isn’t just a slogan — it’s the founding principle of our nation, guaranteed by the Constitution,” the “Irishman” actor said during a speech at the Hands Off Our Vote rally in New York City on Sunday.

“Now there are people, powerful people, who we’ve empowered, who now want to take away our power,” De Niro said.

“Are we going to let them do that?” he asked the crowd.

“Of course we’re not,” the 83-year-old Academy Award winner continued.

“First, we’re going to vote, and we’re going to vote early. Then we’re going to get our family, friends, neighbors and friendly strangers to also answer the call,” he said.

“The Trump administration knows that their policies are not only crazy and cruel — they’re increasingly unpopular,” De Niro said.

“They can see it. They’re not stupid,” he said before pausing and giving a quick chuckle.

“Well, OK, they are very f—ing stupid,” he added.

“They’re stupider than I ever thought, but they recognize what they’re doing is turning away people. They can’t get support from the voters. So what do they do? They try to take our votes away,” De Niro said.

“Keep your f—ing hands off our votes,” the performer said as he went into a call and response with the audience.

“When the weak and spineless Republicans in the House and Senate won’t protect our rights, what are we saying to them? Keep your f—ing hands off our votes.”

“When the Supreme Court rubber stamps voter suppression, what do we say to them? Keep your f—ing hands off our vote! When Trump’s Department of Justice threatens election officials, demands voter rolls, and seizes ballots, what do we say to them? F—ing hands off our vote! When masked and armed ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] thugs stalk our polling places, what do we say to them? Keep your f—ing hands off our vote!” De Niro exclaimed.

“And when that coward, that fucking piece of s—, Donald Trump, tries to take our voice and power away, what do we tell him? Keep your f—ing hands off our vote!

“I think they got the message,” De Niro quipped.

“Take back the House. Take back the Senate. Take back the power. Take back our country,” he said to applause.

De Niro has been one of Trump’s fiercest Hollywood critics, describing him as “sadistic” and a “clown.”

The president has repeatedly ripped De Niro over the years, referring to him as “wacko” and saying the entertainer “suffers from an incurable case of Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

articles.title: Trump uses taxpayer money for propaganda ads
articles.summary: People For the American Way president Svante Myrick criticized President Donald Trump for allegedly using $20 million in taxpayer funds designated for border security to run political advertisements.
articles.body:
President Trump has raised hundreds of millions in PAC money, but he’s using taxpayer dollars to run political ads, apparently to help Republicans who are being dragged down by his historically horrible approval ratings.

You can almost hear the frustrated president demanding that his aides do something — anything — to convince Americans that he is on their side, despite all the evidence that he cares more about his own engorged bank account and metastasizing monuments than he does about struggling families.

The ads being run by the White House are “ sheer propaganda ,” in the words of a former Bush administration official. One ad is basically a rerun of a 2024 campaign ad, but this time it is being paid for by U.S. taxpayers. That is us footing the bill for his campaign ads.

The administration is reportedly using $20 million that is designated by Congress for “border security upgrades, efforts to combat drug trafficking and memorials for officers killed in the line of duty,” according to the Washington Post, to pay for the ads. It is a naked violation of the law, but that is routine for this administration.

Another defining characteristic of the MAGA era is that Trump forces people around him to tell humiliatingly obvious lies in order to stay in his good graces. In this case, that includes a White House official who insists that the new ads aren’t political ads — the spokesperson says the ads are “reminding Americans to love their country.”

That is laughable. Trump has been telling MAGA voters to pretend he is on the ballot. These ads are clearly an effort to boost his personal standing and turn out his most loyal voters.

With Trump’s disapproval rating at over 60 percent, that would probably take better ads than these. In the version that recycles a 2024 campaign ad, Trump’s team didn’t even bother to update the message — Trump is heard pledging to “expel the warmongers from our government.”

Given the “lethality”-obsessed warmonger Trump has installed at the Pentagon, this, too, is laughable. But it’s not very funny to Americans who are suffering from high gas prices and other impacts of Trump’s war on Iran — and who are being asked to pay a mind-boggling amount of money to restock our depleted weapons supply.

Sadly, the political campaign ads are not the only way Trump is taking money from taxpayers to pay for political propaganda.

In September, the White House used government money to launch Trump TV , an official propaganda channel dedicated to streaming a never-ending torrent of Trump’s favorite content — himself.

Days later, the colossally corrupt Trump family business empire sought to trademark the channel’s name. That is just one more way to cash in.

All of this corruption would be terrible news, even if it were not accompanied by attacks on freedom of the press and heavy-handed efforts to squelch media coverage Trump doesn’t like.

Just before the regime launched Trump TV, it banned reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House and presidential events. These major American media outlets were blocked from entering the White House, even as Chinese state media were welcomed to cover President Xi Jinping’s visit.

A federal judge’s temporary restraining order was eventually obeyed by the White House, which has allowed some access to the targeted news outlets, at least until the order expires on Oct. 8.

Meanwhile, the Associated Press is still operating under restrictions imposed by the White House last year as punishment for the news outlet’s decision not to go along with Trump’s unilateral renaming of the Gulf of Mexico.

Congressional Republicans have demonstrated repeatedly their unwillingness to criticize Trump’s corruption and lawbreaking. Even so, his ban on media outlets and use of tax dollars to pay for political ads are egregious enough that they managed to crack — barely and briefly — the wall of silence.

We need much more of that. But we’re not likely to get it right now. Republican officeholders might find it wise to put some distance between themselves and the deeply unpopular president. But who wants to risk his wrath, or jeopardize the chance to get some of the hundreds of millions of dollars he and his allies are dumping into the elections to buy him a two-year reprieve from accountability?

They are hoping they can prove once again the adage that money talks. It’s up to voters to prove that inspired and organized people can beat big money. We have a month. Let’s do it!

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .
